title: The new moon
hookLine: each new month is a small holiday, long honored especially by women

lines: A SLIVER OF MOON AT SUNSET.
cards: A hilltop near Jerusalem, just after sunset, in the days the Mishnah describes. Two people squint at the western sky, looking for the thinnest sliver of moon. They see it.
They hurry to the court in Jerusalem and testify. The judges question them: where was it, which way did it point? When the testimony holds, the court declares it: the new month has begun.
The Mishnah says that news once traveled by torches waved from mountaintop to mountaintop, all the way to the Jews in Babylon. All that, for the first day of a month.

teach.h: ROSH CHODESH: HEAD OF THE MONTH.
teach.b: The first day of every Jewish month has a name: Rosh Chodesh. Rosh means head; chodesh means month, from a root that means new. So the Hebrew month is named for the moon's renewal.
Every month starts with a small holiday. It isn't a day off work, but the synagogue adds an extra prayer service, the psalms of praise called Hallel in a shorter form, and a special Torah reading.
In the Torah, the new moons stand beside the festivals: the Book of Numbers speaks of blowing trumpets "in the day of your gladness, and in your appointed seasons, and in your new moons."
In the Bible's stories, it's a day for a family meal; King Saul notices that David's seat is empty at the new moon feast.
Rosh Chodesh also has a long tie to women.
A midrash tells that when the people built the golden calf, the women refused to hand over their gold jewelry for it, and so they were given the new moons as a holiday of their own.
Jewish law records a custom of women setting aside some work on the day. In recent decades, some Jewish women have gathered in Rosh Chodesh groups to study, sing and talk, month by month.
One more custom: a few days after the new moon, as the moon grows, some Jews go outside at night and say a blessing over it. Why the moon?

teach.h: THE MOON SHRINKS AND COMES BACK.
teach.b: Because it shrinks, disappears, and comes back.
The blessing over the moon makes the comparison itself: it speaks of the Jewish people as destined to be renewed like the moon.

how: On Rosh Chodesh, synagogues add a short Hallel, a Torah reading and an additional service. Some women mark the day with study groups or by setting aside some work, and some communities bless the growing moon a few days later.

games.q: you're one of the women in the wilderness. the men are collecting gold jewelry to make a calf. what do you do?
o: hand over your earrings like everyone else.
games.why: in the midrash, the women refused, and the new moons were given to them as their holiday.

practice: Think about where the moon is right now, even if you can't see it: growing, full, shrinking, or gone dark. Then think of one part of your life that feels like the dark of the moon, something that's gone quiet.
You don't have to fix it; dark is part of the cycle, not the end of it.

wordCard.voice: Rosh Chodesh. The head of the month: the new moon, kept as a small holiday, and long honored as a day for women.

orig.note: Hebrew: head of the month. chodesh comes from chadash, new.

carryVoice: Your line: renew with the moon. Every month gets its own small new beginning. Until tomorrow.
